t: Count Substrings Rearrangeable to Contain word2 — Frequency Window
o: A substring x of word1 is valid iff its multiset of letters covers word2's multiset (then some rearrangement starts with word2). Count all valid substrings. In "abcabc" with word2="abc", every substring of length >= 3 works, giving 10. With |word1| up to 1e5, checking each of O(n^2) substrings naively is too slow; a sliding window that tracks how many distinct letters still fall short of their quota gives a linear solution.
k: Validity depends only on letter counts: x is valid iff count_x[c] >= need[c] for every c in word2.
For each right endpoint, if left is the smallest index making the window valid, exactly left substrings ending at right are valid (starts 0..left-1).

a.n: Approach 1: Brute Force with Running Counts
a.i: Fix a start index and extend the end, maintaining a counter; after each extension check coverage against word2's counts. This is O(n^2 * 26) — clear but too slow for the largest inputs; it establishes the coverage criterion.
s: For each start i, grow a counter over word1[i..j].
Whenever the counter covers need, increment the answer.
a.t: O(n^2 * 26) — every substring endpoint pair is checked.

a.n: Approach 2: Sliding Window with Deficit Counter (Optimal)
a.i: Track 'miss' = number of letters whose window count is still below their quota. Expanding the right end can only decrease miss; shrinking from the left until the window becomes invalid finds, for each right, the minimal valid window. Then every start index before left yields a valid substring, so add left to the answer. Monotonicity of both pointers gives linear time.
s: Compute need and miss = number of letters with need[c] > 0.
For each right, add word1[right], decrementing miss when a letter exactly reaches its quota.
While miss == 0, shrink from the left (incrementing miss when a letter drops below quota).
Add left (the number of valid starts) to the answer.
a.t: O(n) — each index enters and leaves the window at most once, with O(1) updates via the deficit counter.

w: Always present the sliding-window version; the brute force is only for building intuition. Pitfalls: the answer can be ~n^2/2 ≈ 5e9, so use 64-bit / safe accumulation; decrement miss only when a count transitions exactly to its quota (not below). Follow-up: the hard version (3298) asks for substrings rearrangeable to contain word2 as a substring anywhere, solvable with the same window plus a per-letter surplus trick.
